title: Why You're Bad At Classroom Management
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin's central claim is that struggling with classroom management has nothing to do with age, personality, or the roster you're handed — it comes down to two specific deficits: incomplete knowledge and fear of consequences. He explains that SCM strategies work only as an aligned whole, so a teacher who understands some pieces but not others sabotages the entire system. To illustrate the fear half of the equation, he recounts visiting a teacher who could answer every SCM question correctly in training yet fell apart in his own classroom, dissolving into sarcasm and empty warnings because he was afraid that real accountability would make students rebel or complain to parents. Linsin insists those fears are baseless — teachers who actually enforce their plans are respected, not resented. He also names "toxic empathy," the impulse to lower standards to spare student discomfort, as a form of empathy that actively harms kids rather than helping them. The concrete takeaway is that becoming good at classroom management requires comprehensive knowledge paired with the courage to actually apply it.
points: Struggling teachers usually know pieces of an effective approach but haven't learned it comprehensively enough to apply it as an aligned system.
A teacher who can pass a written quiz on strategy can still fail in the room if fear of pushback stops him from actually enforcing it.
Fears about enforcing consequences — that students will rebel, stop liking you, or complain to parents — are described as unfounded.
"Toxic empathy," or lowering standards to spare feelings, is framed as empathy that does real harm to students.
quotes: The reason you’re bad at classroom management is because you don’t know what works and you’re afraid of your students.
These strategies must be aligned to achieve this objective. In other words, they must adhere to a particular approach. Each strategy supports and strengthens the rest.
So why, if he knew what to do, didn’t he do it? Because he was afraid.
First, his fears were and are unfounded. They have absolutely zero merit. In fact, the opposite is true.
To be good at classroom management takes knowledge of what works to create a polite, motivated, and well-behaved classroom from scratch.
It also takes a modicum of courage and belief that all students can succeed despite any and every circumstance.
